hook: We imagine machines building homes on Mars while secure shelter remains elusive here.
readerPromise: Reconsider technological progress through paradise traditions and the institutions that make security usable on Earth.
protectedRevelations: The Second Garden’s detailed constitutional design and prescriptions
visualPlan: Why wait for another planet?: Place imagined robotic shelter-building on Mars beside people awaiting secure homes on Earth. Return attention to the residents on Earth while the distant ambition remains a comparison.
The garden and its gate: Show water, shade and shelter in an old garden plan as answers to ordinary needs. Hold the garden gate between the protected space and the person controlling entry.

What abundance makes possible: Bring a local robot, repairable infrastructure and damaged land into one practical worksite. Keep a resident beside the proposed improvement and the conditions needed to rely on it.
Turn the mirror toward Earth: Compare the distant construction promise with an unfinished repair close to home. End on the Earth-side worksite, leaving its priorities visibly open to choice.

cueChanges.nextVisualChange: Contrast a possible off-world construction site with an ordinary earthly housing need; label the former as imagined visually through context.
Keep water, growing life and a gate together, using a quiet change of viewpoint.
Select one robotics or repair action without presenting speculative abundance as an achieved result.
Return to the earthly place with the gate still visible and the book open beside it.

sentenceIntentions.text: We imagine machines building homes on Mars while secure shelter remains elusive here.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Contrast extraterrestrial ambition with unmet shelter on Earth
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Feel a pointed question about priorities

sentenceIntentions.text: Eden Before Mars uses that contrast to ask what technological ambition is really for.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Name the book's inquiry into technological purpose
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Understand Mars functions as a moral comparison

sentenceIntentions.text: It begins with old dreams of paradise, where water, shelter, and fertile ground answer familiar human needs.
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Recognize enduring human needs within old traditions

sentenceIntentions.text: The same garden wall can offer protection while making someone else the keeper of the gate.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Make the garden boundary both shelter and control

sentenceIntentions.text: The book connects those dreams with robots, public services, ownership, and the possibility of repairing damaged places.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Connect inherited dreams with present technical capacity
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Expect a bridge between myth and political economy

sentenceIntentions.text: It asks how greater productive power could become a life people can actually rely on.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Ask how productivity becomes reliable life conditions
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Question the arrangements between capability and security

sentenceIntentions.text: The promises of progress become more demanding when you compare distant ambitions with needs close to home.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Keep progress's promises open to philosophical scrutiny
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Want to reconsider what ambitious projects are for

sentenceIntentions.text: Begin with paradise as a mirror, and look at the Earth those promises leave waiting.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Return paradise to the Earth still waiting for repair
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Carry a concrete unresolved question about priorities

distinctiveContribution: Paradise traditions and extraterrestrial construction ambitions become a moral comparison with unmet shelter and ecological repair on Earth.
